4999.heavy: 'Long vowels are stressed' (1a): heavy = syllable containing one of the four long vowels â, ee, 8, ô; light = the two short vowels a and u (schwa). 4999.dflt: Words with only short vowels are stressed on their even-numbered syllables (2, 4...), final syllable excluded unless it is the only stress, with main stress on the last non-final stress: e.g. 3-syllable nushkanash stressed on syllable 2 (p. 48); a short-short disyllable takes final stress, e.g. <anúm> 'dog' with the second syllable 'stressed, but... not long' (p. 1, fn. 1); 4- and 6-syllable all-short words get main stress on the antepenult (4th of 6, 2nd of 4).
4999.prule: Every syllable with a long vowel (â /aː/, ee /iː/, 8 /uː/, ô /ãː/) is stressed; within runs of short-vowel syllables (a /a/, u /ə/), counted from the word beginning or from the last long vowel, the even-numbered syllables are stressed (iambic alternation); the word-final syllable is unstressed unless it would be the word's only stress; main (primary) stress falls on the last stressed syllable, i.e. the rightmost non-final stress. Closed syllables do not count as heavy (unlike Lenape).
4999.srule: Secondary stress on every non-primary syllable stressed by the same rules: each long vowel (â, ee, 8, ô) and each even-numbered short vowel counted from the word start or from the preceding long vowel, final syllable excluded; the rightmost (non-final) stress is primary, all earlier ones secondary; adjacent stresses allowed (e.g. <waantog> secondary on syllable 1, primary on 2; wunneetupanatamwe secondary on 2, primary on 4; an all-short six-syllable word is stressed on 2 and 4, not 6).

A sílaba leve é sempre do tipo [CV̆] e a sílaba pesada é sempre do tipo [CVC], [CVː] ou [CVV̯]; (b) um lexema monossílabo é necessariamente constituído por uma sílaba pesada dentre os tipos acima descritos.' 5002.dflt: Not applicable as stated: every lexeme contains exactly one heavy syllable, lexeme-final ('uma sílaba pesada caracteriza sempre o final de um lexema'; 'nunca podem ocorrer seqüências de duas sílabas leves', pp.22-23); no all-light lexeme is described. In casual registers the stressed vowel can shorten (rule (2), p.23); the source is inconsistent on whether the shortened syllable keeps its stress mark: the Moré series on p.23 reads 'Lento / Formal: [ˈkˣaː ˈʔɔn] → Menos lento: [ˈkˣa ˈʔɔn] → Normal: [ˈkˣɔn]' (mark kept), while the p.24 table writes the shortened kˣa and tʃi without ˈ (mark dropped). Either way this is a casual-register phonetic effect, not a stated stress rule for all-light lexemes.
5002.prule: Stress (strong intensity accent plus high pitch) falls on the heavy syllable; a light syllable is unstressed with low pitch. Lexemes are phonotactically restricted to one heavy syllable (CVC, CVː or CVV̯), which is always lexeme-final, optionally preceded by one light CV̆ syllable: /#(σ)σ#/ -> [(σ̀)ˈσ́]. Stress is therefore fully predictable from weight and non-contrastive; in mono- and disyllabic lexemes the weight rule coincides extensionally with final stress (grids '1' and '01'). Stated for the Chapakura family and instantiated with Miguelenho(-Wanyam) forms [mă ˈwín] 'urucum', [mă ˈwíː] 'roubar', [ˈpíʔ] 'dançar', [ˈpiː] 'espinho' (p.23: the acute over the heavy-syllable vowel is the author's high-pitch accent mark, key p.166; ˈ = intensity stress). The author's acoustic means on the last Miguelenho-Wanyam speaker (p.167, geral: light V$ 21.2 dB / 39.6 ST / 120 ms vs heavy VC$ 23.7 dB / 40.6 ST / 148 ms, Vː$ 242 ms) keep the prominence on the heavy syllable; per result (c) p.168 and the summary table p.169, intensity prominence is 'frágil' (plateau-final) overall and after non-glottal onsets but 'resistente' after a glottal-stop onset, while pitch prominence is 'resistente' overall and after a glottal-stop onset but 'frágil' after other onsets.

5005.prule: morphological-domain-initial: stress is assigned not to the word but within morpheme-class domains (verb, nominal stem, polysyllabic suffix, adverb prefixed to or nominal compounded into a verb, polysyllabic pronominal prefix or prefix sequence); primary stress on the first syllable of each such domain, so a word may carry several primaries and a word-initial monosyllabic pronominal prefix is normally unstressed (kat-tjápul-m-al 'I was not smoking'); a partial reduplication overrides this, each copy taking a primary on its initial syllable (púkpúkpanj, át-mekkílkíl-m-inj)
5005.srule: Within each stress domain (morpheme-class domain or partial-reduplication part), secondary stress on every second syllable after the domain-initial primary, but never on a word-final syllable and never on a syllable immediately preceding a primary; with a partial reduplication, secondaries fall on every second syllable on either side of the primaries (át-mekkílkíl-m-inj; kúkutúngunj).

Zorc 1977 p. 50: 'In all dialects studied (except Kuy) stems or derivatives with a closed penult [CVC.CV(C)] are accented on the penult'; p. 243: 'all Bs dialects have penultimate rather than ultimate stress on inherited words with a closed penult... the stress is predictable from the segmental shape'. 5007.heavy: Source states stress is 'not normally weight-sensitive' (p. 51): final syllables closed by a glide or nasal in monomorphemic words do not attract stress (['ii.roi] 'crow', [il.'ko.rom] 'food', ['be.ken] 'smoking platform'). The one weight-like effect is derived: a final closed syllable created by suffix desyllabification ([kil.'tej]) or high-vowel deletion after a nasal ([kil.'ten]) 'satisfies the foot', so stress stays on the syllable that was penultimate before the process rather than shifting to the new penult.
5007.dflt: penultimate (quantity-insensitive rule; not a QS system)
5007.prule: Fixed penultimate stress, quantity-insensitive: a left-headed binary foot is built at the right edge of the (inflected) word and its head is stressed; only the final two syllables are footed, so words of three or more syllables stress the penult. Stress is predictable and non-contrastive; it carries the lexical tone melody.
5007.srule: None: one stress per word. Only the final two syllables of the word are footed ('On trisyllabic words, only the final two syllables are footed', p. 53); four- and five-syllable words 'only have one stress and one tone' (p. 21); syllables before the final two are 'always very short' (p. 49). Corris never uses the term secondary stress. (Productive noun compounds are separate phonological words, each keeping its own stress, with the main stress on the right-hand member, p. 62.)

5007.tone: Barupu is a word-tone language: p. 38 'words belong to tone classes in the lexicon. The five tone classes in Barupu are: L; H; LH; HL and HLH.' Corris calls the system 'a type of pitch accent system' (p. 39) because for most words the lexical melody is attracted to the stressed penult and spreads one syllable right (rules ii a-d, p. 52). A minority of words have an H or HL lexically linked to the penultimate or final syllable; those tones do not move under suffixation (pp. 53-57) and 'lexically assigned final HLs' are the stated exception to contour tones sitting on the stressed syllable (p. 50). Tone is lexical and contrastive; stress is predictable and non-contrastive, diagnosed by slightly higher F0 and longer duration of the penult in L-class words (Figs 2.4-2.7, pp. 48-50).

5008.prule: Accent is lexically contrastive ('O acento é contrastivo'): seven segmentally identical pairs differ only in accent position (initial vs second syllable in every pair: émali/emáli, kédali/kedáli, kápisi/kapísi, ámu/amú, núma/numá, tátali/tatáli, jálanawi/jalánawi). 5008.srule: Words normally bear one accent and no rhythmic alternation is described. Ramirez states only that words with more than one accent are rare and all appear to be of shape CV́CVCV́ (accents on the first and third syllable), e.g. képelá 'sand' vs single-accented képela 'this is earth'; he does not say which of the two accents is primary ('As palavras com mais de um acento são raras e parecem todas do tipo CV́CVCV́').

ev.text: In the majority of Australian languages word stress (or accent) falls on the first syllable, but there are exceptions, one of them being Mathi-Mathi, where the stress in words of more than two syllables falls on various syllables according to certain principles (Hercus 1986d:115). Tyers marks stress and it appears that stress falls regularly on the final syllable of disyllabic words, of which there are numerous examples

karrìp thigh / bebì father / werìte banksia / kannòc waddy / There are a few examples of longer words with stress marked variously. Lindsay also marks stress. In his notation, stress on disyllabic words is predominantly on the second syllable. As with Tyers, stress on longer words appears on various syllables

Only tentative remarks can be made on the phonetics and allophonic variations observed: ... Very noticeable was the long and tense articulation of intervocalic m, particularly when it followed the accented vowel: ... ḏamon meat, dameri sheep and ŋamadjidj white man were therefore transcribed phonetically as [ˈθammɔn], [ˈtammerI] and [ˈŋammatjItj]. ... After an unaccented vowel m did not appear to be geminated: guremug [ˈkurəmUk] possum.

5011.prule: One culminative primary stress per word, no single phonological rule; placement is keyed to stem shape and affix identity: stems of two or more syllables are stressed on the first syllable of the stem; non-syllabic and monosyllabic stems put the stress on the immediately preceding prefix syllable (directive u-, or the syllabic adverbial or object prefix nearest the stem); possessive prefix a- and the 3sg.f object a- are accented; the reflexive+directive sequence x-t- puts stress on the following syllable; suffixes -x, -lal, -nan, -mama, -lx, -pck, -wulx and the distributive plural -max 'draw the accent backward in the word' (the source's term; its examples galikim > galikimx, watul > watulmax show this means toward the end of the word); local-relational suffixes -ba/-yamt likewise 'draw the stress backward in the word' (naika > naika-yamt); demonstratives, personal pronouns and particles are stressed on the first syllable, reduplicated particles on the second element; aga and future alma are 'rarely, if ever, stressed'.
5011.srule: Predictable (non-phonemic) secondary stress on alternate syllables both before and after the primary-stressed syllable; this alternating pattern also tends to run across sequences of words (Dyk & Hymes 1956: 238, section 1).

tn.quote: 那么瓦乡话里的“跟”和“把”两者到底是什么关系呢？从上面的材料看来，瓦乡话的“把”有可能是从西南官话中借来的，理由如下： 1）在古丈瓦乡话里有五个声调，分别为阴平 55，阳平 13，上声 25，去声 33，入声 41。 古丈的西南官话有 4 个声调，分别为阴平 55，阳平 13，上声 41，去声 25。 “把”在中古为上声字，根据对应规律，在古丈瓦乡话中声调应为 25，可是在瓦乡话中“把”的声调为 41，与西南官话的上声调值相同。
tn.translation: So what is the relationship between 跟 and 把 in Waxianghua? From the material above, Waxiang 把 may have been borrowed from Southwestern Mandarin, for these reasons: 1) Guzhang Waxianghua has five tones: yinping 55, yangping 13, shangsheng 25, qusheng 33, rusheng 41. Guzhang Southwestern Mandarin has 4 tones: yinping 55, yangping 13, shangsheng 41, qusheng 25. 把 was a shangsheng word in Middle Chinese; by the regular correspondence its tone in Guzhang Waxianghua should be 25, but in Waxianghua 把 has tone 41, the same as the Southwestern Mandarin shangsheng value.

5018.dq: Primary stress is assigned to the penultimate (second last) vowel of a word with secondary stress on every second vowel to the left.
5018.heavy: Not stated as weight by the source; stated as vowel counting: 'Sequences of two identical vowels /ii/, /ee/, /aa/, /oo/ and /uu/ are usually each realized as a single phonetically long vowel.... such reduced double vowels still bear primary stress, as expected for penultimate vowels.' Equivalent heavy syllable = one containing a double (long) vowel or two-vowel sequence (VV); closed CVC syllables are not heavy (fulan [ˈfʊla̟n], tikan [ˈtikæn] keep penult stress).
5018.prule: As stated: primary stress on the penultimate vowel of the word, every vowel counting one, a phonemic double vowel /ii ee aa oo uu/ (realized as one long vowel) counting as two; so a word-final double vowel carries primary stress (kiis-aan [ˌkiːˈsaˑŋ] 'teeth', iluk-aan [ˌʔɪlʊˈkaŋ] 'nose', ikim-aan [ˌʔɪkiˈmaŋ] 'chin', oet-aat [ʔɔɛˈt̪æːt̪] 'vein', hare wee [ˌharˈβ̞ɛː] 'wet rice field') while words with a short final vowel stress the penultimate syllable (fulan [ˈfʊla̟n] 'moon', tikan [ˈtikæn] 'year', lobu [ˈlobʊ] 'mud', isa [ˈʔisa] 'one'). On surface syllables (the catalog's unit): stress the final syllable if it contains a double/long vowel (CVV), otherwise the penult; closed CVC finals are not heavy. Cued by higher pitch and length.
5018.srule: Secondary stress on every second vowel to the left of the primary (binary alternation leftward, counted in vowels; a double vowel counts two): ulit-aat [ˌʔʊlˑˈt̪æt̪] 'skin', iluk-aan [ˌʔɪlʊˈkaŋ] 'nose', usan milis [ˌʔʊsa̟nˈmɪlɪs] 'drizzle'; with the suffix allomorphs -aan/-aat the bare stem's stressed syllable keeps a secondary stress (p. 39).

The placement of stress in Ojibwa (including Saulteaux) can be satisfactorily explained in a fairly straightforward fashion and there can be several stressed syllables within a word. There are three basic rules for stress assignment (as put forward by Voorhis et al 1976 and Cote 1984): 1) Each syllable with a long vowel will be stressed. 2) The last syllable of every word is obligatorily stressed. 3) Every second syllable in a sequence of syllables with short vowels will be stressed

5022.prule: Conflict between the two reachable first-hand descriptions. Miller 2018 (eight Manitoba Saulteaux speakers, 24 h of recordings, impressionistic): the only consistent prominence is on the final syllable of every noun and verb (rise in pitch and intensity), in isolation and inside sentences; no consistent primary or secondary stress elsewhere, and neither the traditional exhaustive-foot analysis nor Hayes' non-exhaustive analysis predicts what is heard; the author leaves open whether final prominence is word stress or a boundary effect. Logan 2001:11 (Saskatchewan Saulteaux, restating Voorhis et al. 1976 and Cote 1984): every long-vowel syllable is stressed, the last syllable of every word is obligatorily stressed, and every second syllable in a run of short-vowel syllables is stressed, the remaining short vowels reducing or eliding; no primary stress designated (explicitly left aside). The two descriptions agree only that the final syllable is prominent.

5023.prule: Stratum-conditioned, hence lexically determined, word stress. Hebrew/Aramaic-component words (the whole of Weinberg's material) are 'gewöhnlich' stressed on the penultimate syllable, the Ashkenazic retraction from the Hebrew final syllable (berochaus < berakhót); the lexicon marks stress on a headword only when another syllable of a Hebrew word carries it (e.g. aumerbart), and the stress of a word in isolation is 'normalerweise fest' or varies with register (informal penult vs formal 'grammatische Betonung', berochaus ~ berochaus). The Germanic component is outside Weinberg's material; Katz 1993's pan-Yiddish statement gives it root-bound stress. No syllable-count or weight rule covers the language: position follows the word's component, the register, and, within the Hebrew component, the individual word.

5025.dq: Watters (2002: 23-4) reports that in bisyllabic and polysyllabic words with monomoraic syllables there is "no discernable stress" but that in trisyllabic forms "there is discernable stress on the final syllable". 5025.dloc: LAPSyD record 10012 (http://lapsyd.ddl.cnrs.fr/lapsyd/index.php?data=view&code=10012), Stress field, complete text quoted (reporting Watters 2002: 23-24); tone domain: Watters 1971: 42, sect. IV.A Tone: The Basic System.
5025.heavy: Carried text (LAPSyD on Watters 2002: 23-24): 'final long syllables' as against 'monomoraic syllables'; the primary's wording of 'long' is not in the carried text. Watters' own weight definition, first-hand in the 2003 sketch (Watters 2003: 686, excerpt): "The basic syllable in Kham is (C)(G)V(X), where ‘G’ is a glide and ‘*X’ is a consonant or a vowel. Only the nucleus is obligatory. The presence of a glide adds no weight to the syllable. Weight is determined solely by the rhyme; the presence of X always creates a heavy syllable. Where X is a vowel of the same quality as V, the result is a long vowel (V:), and where X is a vowel of different quality, the result is a diphthong (VV). Where X is a consonant, V is necessarily short. In terms of syllable weight and rhythm groups, then, V:, VV, and VC have the same weight — all are bimoraic. The minimal word in Kham is bimoraic, while the minimal syllable is monomoraic." So a non-monomoraic ('long') syllable in Watters' terms is any bimoraic rhyme: V:, VV or VC; hence CVV+CVC rather than CVV alone. Watters 1971: 57 (about pitch, not stress) groups CVC and CV: the same way: "Any CVC or CV: syllable in a poly-syllabic stem is higher in pitch than an otherwise identical CV syllable."
5025.dflt: no discernible stress in bisyllabic/polysyllabic words of monomoraic syllables, except that trisyllabic forms show discernible stress on the final syllable
5025.prule: Non-contrastive stress conditioned by syllable length (Watters 2002: 23-24): stress falls on the long syllable, whether it is the final syllable (phətú: 'wool coat') or, where the first syllable is long ('which is somewhat rare'), on that long syllable rather than the final one (ká:sa 'lightly', phó:sa 'lung', bé:pari 'trader'); in trisyllabic morphemes of open short syllables stress is on the final syllable (buchulá 'adze', bokolá 'tree bark'); in bisyllabic morphemes of open short syllables there is no discernible stress placement (kata, baza, gohga). Stress 'is not to be equated with high pitch'; tone (melody x register) is the contrastive word prosody. LAPSyD's summary adds that Kham 'is interpreted as having no function for stress' and that 'these perceptions of stress may be illusory' (wording not found in the book's indexed text).

5025.tone: Kham is a word-tone language. Watters 1971: 42 (first-hand, scan of the SIL file): "The primary components of tone in Kham are those of pitch pattern and voice register. The domain of tone is the phonological word... In general, the first morpheme of a word determines the voice register of the word, and the last morpheme of a word determines the pitch pattern of the word." Two pitch patterns (pattern 1 marked, pattern 2 unmarked) x two voice registers (tense vs lax); LAPSyD, citing Watters 2002: 32, gives the same as a 4-way contrast (falling high-low vs low pitch pattern, crossed with breathy phonation). Watters 1985 (LTBA 8(2)) treats the tone as emergent word tone and states no stress rule. On stress the only statement is the carried Watters 2002: 23-24 remark: no functional stress; perceived final stress on long final syllables and in trisyllabic forms; possibly illusory. First-hand confirmation in Watters 2003: 687-688 (house cache, 0 occurrences of 'stress' in the 22-page chapter): "There are two contrastive melodies — a marked, ‘accented’ tone (T1), and an unmarked, ‘neutral’ tone (T2). Voice register has a modifying effect on the fundamental frequencies of tone bearing units, dividing the pitch range into ‘upper’ and ‘lower’ frequencies." and on the domain: "In some languages, the primary domain is the ‘word’, and in others like Kham, the primary domain is the word base (roots and derivational morphemes). Inflectional suffixes manifest a separate tonal character."…
